e.t: Bealoth is a Hebrew place-name, identifying a location rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, once in Joshua 15:24 and once in 1 Kings 4:16. The available biblical renderings preserve it as “Bealoth,” so its ordinary meaning is the name of a place. The exact significance of that location in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

This Hebrew word describes something that is reddish in color. It functions as a color term, identifying a visible red or red-tinged appearance rather than naming an object or action. It occurs six times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all within Leviticus, where it helps describe visible conditions examined under Israel’s laws. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the thing being described, but its basic sense remains a reddish appearance.

Bera is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, this word appears only once, and its English rendering is consistently “Bera.” Because it functions as a name, its meaning is primarily identification: it distinguishes one person from others in the biblical record. The surrounding verse provides the specific historical setting, but the word itself serves as a personal designation.

This Hebrew word describes something as “high,” indicating elevation or a position above others. It appears twice in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, both times in Psalm 68, where it functions as a descriptive term rather than naming an action or person. The available usage consistently renders it as “high,” so its central idea is elevated height or status. Its precise force in each verse depends on the surrounding wording and context.

Gudgodah is a Hebrew place-name, rendered “Gudgodah.” It refers to a named location rather than describing an action, quality, or person. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Deuteronomy 10:7. The available information identifies the name and its use as a location, but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain the place’s geography or significance. Its precise role in that verse therefore depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew word means “pride,” referring to an elevated view of oneself or one’s status. It functions as a noun naming this attitude or condition. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, at Daniel 4:37, so its ordinary scriptural use is represented by that single occurrence. The surrounding verse provides the specific setting, while the word itself identifies pride as the subject being named.

This Hebrew word means “treasurer,” naming a person entrusted with overseeing money or valuable possessions. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at Ezra 1:8, so its normal biblical use is represented by that single occurrence. The term identifies an office or responsibility rather than an action: it refers to the person who keeps account of and manages what has been entrusted to him. The surrounding verse supplies the specific situation in which the title is used.

e.t: This Hebrew word is the personal name “Gaal,” identifying a man in the book of Judges. It functions as a proper name rather than as a general description or action. The name occurs nine times in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, all within Judges 9, from Judges 9:26 through 9:41. Several recorded uses place Gaal in speech-related settings, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain each particular scene. As a lexical word, its supported meaning is therefore the person’s name “Gaal.”

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “joints,” the places where parts meet or are joined. It functions as a noun naming those connected points. It occurs three times in the Old Testament corpus, appearing once each in 1 Kings 22:34, 2 Chronicles 18:33, and Isaiah 41:7. In the two accounts involving 1 Kings and 2 Chronicles, it is treated as the object of related statements, reinforcing that the word identifies a particular part or location rather than an action.

Darkon is a Hebrew personal name, preserved in English as “Darkon.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus: once in Ezra 2:56 and once in Nehemiah 7:58. Because no short definition or descriptive meaning is provided, its supported sense is the name itself, with the surrounding passage needed to clarify the person or family identified there.

Hodiah is a Hebrew personal name, used to identify people rather than to describe an action or quality. It occurs four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing once in 1 Chronicles and three times in Nehemiah. In each recorded rendering, it is represented as “Hodiah,” so its role is chiefly a person’s name. The occurrences are found at 1 Chronicles 4:19 and Nehemiah 10:10, 13, and 18.

This Hebrew word describes defeating or overwhelming an opposing person or people, with English renderings such as “destroy” and “discomfited.” It presents a forceful action that leaves the opponent unable to withstand what comes against them. The word occurs 16 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its central idea is established across several passages rather than belonging to only one setting. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context, but it consistently points to decisive defeat or ruin rather than a mild disturbance.

This word expresses a limited idea whose exact sense depends on its context. It appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Ezra 6:11. No direct English gloss or short definition is available here, so its precise meaning cannot be stated more narrowly without adding information that is not provided. The word functions within that single verse, and the surrounding verse text is needed to explain its force there accurately.

This Hebrew word refers to a “weapon,” an object used for fighting. It functions as a noun, naming an implement rather than an action or quality. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Deuteronomy 23:13, so its normal lexical sense is narrowly attested in this corpus. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain exactly how the weapon is being discussed there; the word itself identifies the implement.

“Oppressed” is the supported meaning of this Hebrew word. It describes someone who has been subjected to unjust treatment or hardship, functioning as a description of a person in need of justice. The word occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Isaiah 1:17. Its precise force in that verse belongs to the surrounding passage, but its central idea is a person experiencing oppression rather than one acting freely or securely.

This Hebrew word expresses shame or being ashamed. It describes the condition of someone exposed to disgrace, humiliation, or defeat, and it can also describe bringing shame upon someone. In the Old Testament, it occurs 17 times, including passages where people who oppose God or His servants are put to shame. The word therefore points to public or personal disgrace rather than merely feeling embarrassed. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on whether the sentence describes someone experiencing shame or causing another person to suffer it.

This Hebrew word is a personal name, rendered “Harhaiah.” It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Nehemiah 3:8. Because no lexical definition or explanatory verse text is available here, its underlying name meaning cannot be stated reliably. Its role is therefore best understood as identifying the person named Harhaiah in that passage.

This Hebrew word means “little,” describing something limited in size or amount. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 1 Kings 20:27, so its normal meaning is represented by a single occurrence rather than a broad range of passages. In a sentence, it functions as a descriptive term, identifying something as small or not great in extent. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording and context.

Jaazaniah is a personal name, used to identify a person rather than to describe an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears four times and is consistently rendered “Jaazaniah.” The name occurs in 2 Kings, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel, showing that it belongs to named individuals mentioned across several passages. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself does not establish which particular person is intended or what that person did.

Jediael is a personal name used for individuals in the Old Testament. It identifies people recorded in genealogical and military lists, rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs six times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in 1 Chronicles, including passages about family lines, warriors, and gatekeepers. Its precise significance as a name is not defined here, but its repeated use consistently functions as a person's identifying name.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “hand.” It refers to a physical hand and functions as a naming word within Old Testament sentences. The word occurs six times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing across First Samuel, First Chronicles, Second Chronicles, and Ezekiel. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central lexical sense remains “hand.”

Iscah is a personal name, rendered as “Iscah.” It identifies one individual rather than describing an action, object, or quality. This Hebrew word occurs once, in Genesis 11:29, so its ordinary meaning is limited to this name rather than a broader vocabulary concept. The name itself does not provide a general definition or a wider category of meaning; the surrounding verse is needed to explain the person’s role in that passage.

This Hebrew word refers to an “abundance”—a plentiful amount or surplus. It is used twice in the Old Testament, in Isaiah 15:7 and Jeremiah 48:36, showing that it describes something substantial that can be carried away, possessed, or lost. Its basic sense concerns the presence of plentiful resources rather than a specific object. The surrounding verse determines exactly what abundant thing is being discussed.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “lies”—words or claims that are not true. It commonly functions as the object of speech, describing what someone says or presents falsely. In the Old Testament, it appears 29 times, including passages in Psalms, Proverbs, Ezekiel, Amos, and Daniel. Its use also connects false speech with misleading people and, in one setting, with actions associated with death. The surrounding verse determines whether the focus is deception, false testimony, or an untruthful message.

This Hebrew noun means “bag,” naming a container used to hold or carry something. It appears six times in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, always as a concrete object rather than an action or quality. Its occurrences include references in Deuteronomy, Proverbs, Isaiah, and Micah. In a sentence, it identifies the bag itself—the object being mentioned. Its precise significance in any one verse comes from the surrounding sentence.

The word appears 40 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, from Exodus through Zechariah, showing repeated use in instructions, worship, commerce, and ordinary accounts. Its use is especially connected with giving or handling a measured amount, so the surrounding passage identifies what is being measured and why.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to an “advantage,” identifying what is favorable or useful in a situation. It functions as the thing being considered when a passage speaks about what someone gains, possesses, or finds worthwhile. The word occurs three times in the Old Testament, all in Ecclesiastes, showing a focused use rather than a broadly distributed term. Its occurrences can also appear in contexts involving what is given or received.

This Hebrew word refers to "gleanings," the material gathered by gleaning. It functions as a naming word for what is left to be gathered from a field. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, both times in Leviticus. Its two recorded uses connect it with the land and field harvest, helping show that it names gathered produce rather than a person or an action. The precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word refers to a spring or fountain—a place where water flows from the ground. It appears three times in the Old Testament, in Ecclesiastes and Isaiah. Its uses are connected with images of water and refreshment, though the precise force in each verse depends on the surrounding wording. The word therefore points to a natural source of flowing water rather than to water in general.

This Hebrew word means “Median,” serving as a name or identifying term for someone or something associated with the Median people. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at Daniel 5:31. Because the available information gives the word’s identifying sense but not the verse text, its precise role in that sentence must be understood from Daniel 5:31 and its surrounding passage. The word itself functions chiefly to identify Median origin or association.

Its precise significance is therefore that of a proper name identifying this individual, rather than a general term describing an action, quality, or object.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “oak,” referring to a strong, established tree. It is used for a particular tree standing in the land, and it appears in scenes involving people, burial, worship, and speech. The word occurs 13 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing a recurring biblical reference to oaks as recognizable places or landmarks. Its precise significance in any individual passage depends on the surrounding context, but its ordinary meaning is an oak tree.

This Hebrew noun refers to “destruction”—the condition or outcome of being brought down, ruined, or made desolate. It describes a serious consequence rather than an action word, and it appears in passages from Psalms, Proverbs, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. In Proverbs, its repeated use presents destruction as the end associated with certain ways of living, while its appearance in Jeremiah belongs to a passage describing devastation. The word occurs 11 times in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus. This Hebrew word refers to a grate or grating: a structured surface made with openings. It is used six times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Exodus, for a component of the tabernacle’s furnishings. As a noun, it names the physical object itself rather than an action or quality. The repeated use in descriptions of the altar shows that the word belongs to the practical vocabulary of constructing and arranging sacred equipment.

This Hebrew noun means “store,” referring to a place where goods or supplies are kept. It is used for designated storage places connected with buildings, cities, or royal activity. The word occurs seven times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing a consistent reference to a storage location rather than to the act of storing. Its precise role in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew word means “taking,” describing the act of taking something. It functions as an action term rather than naming a person, place, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Chronicles 19:7. Because it appears only once and no broader definition is provided, “taking” is the clearest supported sense. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording and passage.

This Hebrew word means “drop,” referring to a small amount of liquid or another substance. It functions as a concrete noun describing something that falls or exists in a very small quantity. The word occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Isaiah 40:15. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the simple term “drop.”

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to a ward or guard: a place kept under watch, or the guarding assigned there. It is used 22 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including settings connected with imprisonment, confinement, and watchfulness. Its central idea is protection or supervision under appointed oversight. Depending on the sentence, it may describe the guarded place itself or the responsibility of keeping watch. The surrounding verse determines which aspect is emphasized.

This Hebrew word means “push,” describing forceful thrusting against something. It appears twice in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, both times in Exodus 21, where the surrounding law discusses an animal’s repeated or dangerous behavior. Its basic sense is therefore an active, forceful shove or thrust, rather than a general movement. The exact force intended in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but “push” is the supported meaning for this word.

This Hebrew word means “Break,” describing an action rather than naming an object or person. It occurs twice in the Old Testament corpus, in Jeremiah 4:3 and Hosea 10:12. It functions as a verb, expressing the act of breaking. The word is therefore best understood as a direct action term, while its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording.

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to “vengeance”—the carrying out of retribution against wrongdoing or injury. It describes vengeance as something that can be given or carried out, including acts attributed to God and judgments against nations. The word occurs 27 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing a recurring biblical concern with justice and repayment rather than a passing idea. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and who is presented as administering it.

This Hebrew word means “battle” and functions as a term naming such an event. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, in Isaiah 9:5. The available rendering consistently gives “battle,” supporting this central sense. Because the word appears only once and the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise force in that passage must be understood from the larger context of Isaiah 9:5 rather than from the word alone.

This word means “yet.” It marks something that continues or remains the case, often carrying the thought forward despite what has just been said. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Ecclesiastes 4:2–3. Its precise force in each sentence depends on the surrounding wording, but its normal function is to express continuing comparison or a further point in the argument. (Ecclesiastes 4:2; 4:3)

This Hebrew word describes abuse or mistreatment, especially treatment that harms, humiliates, or takes unfair advantage of someone. It can also express mocking or harsh treatment, as in the account of Balaam and the donkey. In some renderings it appears as “am,” but “abuse” is the clearer meaning clue available here. The word occurs 20 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including passages about gleaning and Israel’s hardened response to God’s signs. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

Assir is a Hebrew personal name, rendered as “Assir.” It identifies a particular person rather than expressing a general quality, action, or object. This name occurs five times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing once in Exodus and four times in 1 Chronicles. Because the available passages do not include their verse text, the name’s specific role in each genealogy or listing cannot be described here. Its consistent rendering indicates that it functions as a name throughout these occurrences.

e.t: This Hebrew word is a personal name: “Phichol.” It identifies a particular person rather than expressing a general action, quality, or object. It appears in Genesis 21:22, Genesis 21:32, and Genesis 26:26.

This Hebrew word describes dividing—separating something into parts or portions. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Daniel 7:25, so its normal lexical meaning is supported by a single occurrence rather than a broad range of passages. In that sentence, it functions as an action or process involving division. The precise force of the word in Daniel 7:25 depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here.

This Hebrew noun means “iron,” referring to the metal itself. It names a material rather than an action, person, or quality. In the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, the word occurs 20 times, all in Daniel, where it is used repeatedly in the account recorded there. Its basic meaning remains consistent: iron as a material mentioned in the text. The surrounding verse determines the specific significance of iron in each passage.

This Hebrew verb describes being “forced” or “restrained,” expressing a person or action held back from moving freely. It can refer to controlling oneself or being compelled by circumstances, so its exact emphasis depends on the sentence. The word occurs seven times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including descriptions of people who restrain themselves and situations in which someone is driven to act under pressure.

The word occurs 22 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, across 22 verses, so it functions as a name rather than a general description or action. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This Hebrew word means “Zophim,” functioning as a proper name rather than an ordinary descriptive term. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Numbers 23:14, and the English rendering preserves it as “Zophim.” Because no verse text or explicit definition is available here, the safest understanding is simply the name itself; its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding biblical context.

e.t: This word refers to “cassia,” a named material or commodity. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, once in Exodus and once in Ezekiel. In Ezekiel, it functions as an object connected with giving, showing that the word can identify something offered or transferred. Its meaning remains focused and concrete: it names cassia rather than describing an action, quality, or person. The surrounding verse determines the precise role cassia plays in each passage.

This Hebrew word expresses being “jealous.” It is used to describe a jealous response or attitude toward someone or something. In the Old Testament, it occurs 33 times across 28 verses, so it represents a recurring biblical expression rather than a rare term. Its exact force—whether describing God or a human—depends on the sentence and surrounding passage within its context.

Kishion is a proper place-name, referring to a location named in the Old Testament. It is not presented here as a general word describing an idea, action, or quality. The name appears twice in the Hebrew Bible’s recorded Old Testament occurrences, both in Joshua: Joshua 19:20 and Joshua 21:28. Since no verse text is included here, the name’s precise role in each passage depends on the surrounding context, but its basic sense is the location called Kishion.

This Hebrew word means “decked,” describing an action performed on something. It functions as a verb rather than naming a person, object, or quality. The word occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Proverbs 7:16. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, its precise force in that sentence cannot be described further.
